# HTML Button: Redirect on click

You have an `<input type="submit">` element, and you want it to act like a link that navigates the browser to another URL when clicked. The code snippet you providedâ`<input type='submit' name='submit' value='Register' class='register' />`âis fundamentally different from an anchor tag. An `<input>` of type `submit` is designed to trigger form submission logic, not navigation. To make it redirect, you must either embed a URL within the element or handle the click event via JavaScript.

### Using the FormAction Attribute

The most direct way to achieve a redirection without writing custom scripts is to leverage the `formaction` attribute. This works similarly to how `<button>` elements function in modern HTML5 standards. By adding `formaction="https://example.com/register"` to your input, the browser will navigate to that URL when the button is clicked.

However, there is a critical catch: this only works if the `<input>` sits inside a `<form>` element with an action attribute of its own. If you place the input outside of any form, or if the parent form has a different action, the `formaction` attribute might not behave as expected depending on the browser's default handling of orphaned submit buttons.

### Leveraging JavaScript for Flexibility

In many modern applications, relying solely on HTML attributes is insufficient because you need to handle state changes before redirecting. For instance, you might want to verify that a session exists or clear specific data before sending the user away. In these scenarios, attaching an `onclick` event handler is the standard approach.

You can attach an inline event handler directly to the element:

```html
<input type="submit" name="submit" value="Register" class="register" onclick="window.location.href = 'https://example.com/register'; return false;" />
```

The `return false` part is crucial here. Without it, the browser might still attempt to submit the form if the input is nested inside a `<form>` tag. If your goal is strictly redirection and you do not intend for any data to be POSTed to a server, this inline method provides immediate control over the navigation flow.

Alternatively, using event listeners offers a cleaner separation of concerns:

```javascript
document.querySelector('.register').addEventListener('click', function() {
  window.location.href = 'https://example.com/register';
});
```

This approach allows you to attach multiple handlers if needed and keeps your HTML markup clean. It also makes it easier to add conditional logic, such as checking for errors or loading additional data via AJAX before performing the redirect.

### Choosing Between Input Types

While `<input type="submit">` is valid, consider switching to `<button>` if you are dealing with complex UI logic. The `<button>` element can exist outside of a form and still carry an `onclick` handler or a `formaction` attribute effectively. Furthermore, many CSS frameworks and utility libraries treat buttons differently than inputs regarding styling and focus states.

If you are working within a Laravel project, you might find that Blade templates offer specific directives to handle these redirects cleanly without cluttering your view with JavaScript logic. For example, using the `redirect()` helper function in a controller and passing a URL back to the view, or utilizing `url()` helpers, ensures consistency across your application's navigation patterns.

Ultimately, the choice depends on whether you need the element to trigger a form submission or simply navigate the user. If it is purely a navigation trigger, treating the element as a linkâeven if it renders as a buttonâis often the most robust solution for ensuring consistent behavior across different browsers and devices.
